lesson.title: Más o Menos: The Guess-My-Number Game
lesson.subject: spanish

contentBlocks.text: You can count to cien and pick a number out of a listening grid. Today you'll play a game with those numbers: one person thinks of a secret number, the other guesses, and two little words — más and menos — say whether to guess higher or lower.

You already met más last week, where it meant 'plus' in a math fact. It has a second job: it also means 'more.' In the guessing game, más means 'my number is higher — guess up.' Its opposite is menos, meaning 'less' — 'my number is lower, guess down.'

Here's one round. The secret number is 58.

— Pienso en un número entre uno y cien. (I'm thinking of a number between one and one hundred.)
— ¿Cincuenta? (Fifty?) — Más. (Higher.)
— ¿Ochenta? (Eighty?) — Menos. (Lower.)
— ¿Sesenta? (Sixty?) — Menos. (Lower.)
— ¿Cincuenta y cinco? (Fifty-five?) — Más. (Higher.)
— ¿Cincuenta y ocho? (Fifty-eight?) — ¡Sí! (Yes!)

Each clue tells the guesser which way to move next.

A smart guesser starts in the middle and cuts the leftover range in half each time. Start at cincuenta (50). If you hear más, the number is 51-100, so guess in the middle of that — maybe setenta y cinco (75). If you hear menos, it's 1-49, so guess around veinticinco (25). Each clue chops your job roughly in half, and you can corner any number between uno and cien in about seven guesses.

You just used más and menos to zero in on a hidden number — real back-and-forth conversation in Spanish, not a worksheet. Tomorrow your numbers go shopping: prices and quantities with play money all the way to cien.

objectives: Use más ('higher') and menos ('lower') as clues in a guess-my-number game
Give the correct clue by comparing a secret number to a guess, both in the 1-100 range
Explain the halving strategy: start at cincuenta and cut the range in half with each clue
materialsNeeded: A partner or family member to play the guessing game with
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Remind the child that más meant 'plus' last week; today it also means 'more / higher,' and menos is its opposite, 'less / lower.'
2. Play one slow round yourself: you think of a secret number 1-100, the child guesses, and you answer only más or menos until they get it.
3. Swap roles — the child picks the secret and gives the clues while you guess, so they practice producing más/menos, not just hearing them.
4. Teach the halving strategy: start at cincuenta, then aim for the middle of whatever range is left.
5. Play the speed-drill activity together (the secret is always sesenta).
6. Complete the worksheet.
7. Preview tomorrow: prices and play money to cien.
differentiationTips: Struggling: keep guesses and secrets to the tens only (cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa) so the comparison is just 'which tens word is bigger'
Ready for more: challenge them to catch any secret number 1-100 in seven guesses or fewer by halving the range every time, saying each guess as a full Spanish number

This lesson's guessing game is a live two-person spoken exchange, so — unlike Tuesday's listening grid — it doesn't depend on the audio-recording gap noted elsewhere this week (open decision, expansion-plan-2026-09.md §12.9); any partner can give the clues
teacherGuide.answerKey: más means 'higher, guess up'; menos means 'lower, guess down.' For a secret of sesenta (60): guesses of treinta, cuarenta, and cincuenta all get más; guesses of setenta, ochenta, noventa, and cien all get menos. Strategy: start at cincuenta and aim for the middle of the range left after each clue — any number 1-100 falls in about seven guesses.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Delivers the scope-and-sequence's Day 3 activity (guess-my-number with más/menos) under WA-WL-2015.1.2. The receptive side — hearing más or menos and adjusting the next guess — is interpretive listening under game pressure, while the halving strategy quietly connects to the number sense the whole week builds. It also recycles más from week 4 in a new meaning, the kind of spiraling the scope-and-sequence's band notes call for.
